ideas.idea: The nobody-idle rule is a utilisation-oriented org design (Org Topologies' Resource topology) that optimises for keeping people busy rather than for delivery flow.
ideas.note: Resource topology's purpose is that each unit is 100% utilized.

ideas.idea: Spreading developers across two or three squads forces multitasking and context switching, inflating work in progress; multitasking does not work and focus is needed to deliver faster.
ideas.note: Hurtado: limit the number of things we do; multitasking does not work.

ideas.idea: Little's Law (cycle time = WIP / throughput) means the extra WIP lengthens cycle time.
As utilisation approaches 100%, queue and lead times grow exponentially or towards infinity.
ideas.note: Library says everyone can be busy while work gets slower; no queueing-curve or exponential/infinite claim.

ideas.idea: Communication overhead grows non-linearly with team interdependencies, so fragmenting 60 engineers across nine squads cuts effective output.
ideas.note: Jones models overhead against team size (Dpeak); applying it to cross-squad membership is added.

ideas.idea: Task switching and interruptions carry measurable cognitive costs, raising error rates.
ideas.note: Rogers & Monsell task switching; Altmann et al. interruption sequence errors.

ideas.idea: Optimising each part (keeping every person loaded) in isolation can make the whole system's flow worse.
The carried-over points accumulate as a queue, and the system reacts to that accumulation, not only to new input.
ideas.note: SSDL accumulations brief.

ideas.idea: Planning 40 when the team reliably ships 25 means the plan ignores empirical capacity; the plan is wrong, not the team.
ideas.note: Consistent underdelivery = taking on more than historical performance supports.

ideas.idea: Plan each sprint to what squads actually finish (about 25 points, from recent history).
Firm commitments beyond historical performance lead to burnout, poor quality, loss of trust and gaming.
Respect for people means sustainable pace; an exhausted developer or team is a recipe for disaster.
Overload (time pressure, high workload, simultaneous tasks) is a leading error precursor, so the bugs and the outage come from the same conditions as the overflow.
ideas.note: DOE top error precursors.

ideas.idea: The organisation gets exactly the performance it is set up to get; quality depends on the load leadership sets, so it is not 'engineering's problem'.
Leaders create the conditions for success or failure and are responsible for changing them.
Paying leads on story-point throughput invites Goodhart gaming: the people estimating points will inflate them rather than deliver more.
A quantified output target leads people to neglect unmeasured quality (testing, review), trading quality for visible quantity.
Individual goals in interdependent teamwork backfire; group goals are preferable, especially when leads share developers.
Goals seen as unreasonable or impossible lose their motivating effect.
Strong commitment to difficult goals reduces organisational citizenship such as reviewing colleagues' work or helping other squads.
Productivity-only bonuses (alongside disciplining honest mistakes) are flawed cultural controls against error.
Pay motivates strongly only under conditions (high trust, accurately measurable individual performance, big differentials, no penalties for good performance) this target lacks.
ideas.note: Lawler.

ideas.idea: Production pressure crowds out prevention and thoroughness (production beats prevention without strong leadership; efficiency-thoroughness trade-off).
ideas.note: Merges DOE production-vs-prevention and Hollnagel's ETTO (cited in LFUO).

ideas.idea: Tension: goal-setting research favours difficult, specific goals, while its own cautions and Goodhart's law warn targets get gamed and narrow focus.
ideas.note: K draws the pro side from the OPL OKR page (open-practice-library.md:13600). A's 'stretch works for simple tasks' rider is not in the library.

ideas.idea: Tension: money raises motivation when tied to goals, yet self-determination research finds extrinsic rewards lower intrinsic motivation.
Let squads take part in setting any hard goal, because participation raises commitment.
Tie goals or rewards to shared customer or business outcomes (churn, reliability) rather than squad output.
ideas.note: Outcome over output plus group goals.

ideas.idea: Replace points as the measure with flow and quality measures (lead/cycle time, carryover, escaped defects, time to restore), reviewed rather than paid against.
ideas.note: Track work-item metrics, not utilisation.

ideas.idea: Suspend or remove the link between the throughput target and squad leads' bonuses.
ideas.note: Follows from DOE flawed-controls list and goal cautions.

ideas.idea: Story points and velocity are a forecasting tool, not a performance target.
ideas.note: Sprint backlog is a good-faith forecast.

ideas.idea: A feature a week is an output target; more output does not mean more outcomes, and investing to raise output is suspect.
Marketing and engineering are both right: speed and quality compete for one capacity and nobody owns the trade-off, so it gets settled by default.
ideas.note: CAIB conflicting goals of cost, schedule and safety, applied.

ideas.idea: Schedule pressure adds small pieces of risk that accumulate unnoticed until the programme operates too close to its margins.
The danger point is a culture where nobody will say a date can't be met.
Aggressive schedules can be healthy as long as the pressure they put on safety and quality is watched.
Separate the authority to hold a release from those who manage the growth schedule (independent technical authority).
Give each product line one Product Owner who orders the backlog; marketing argues its case with that owner and the CEO backs the call.
Prioritise jointly by cost of delay (WSJF) rather than a weekly output quota.
Allocate capacity 70/20/10 across growth features, debt remediation and infrastructure/reliability.
ideas.note: Letaw's project priority matrix (letaw-handbook-sweng-methods.md:1047) balances scope/time/cost; no capacity split.

ideas.idea: Neither side has shown why customers churn (people keep using faulty software if it gives enough value); test it against account incident history before choosing a side.
Engineering is right that bugs and instability are driving churn.
ideas.note: No source links defects to SaaS churn; Jones points the other way.

ideas.idea: Shortcuts accumulate technical debt that slows later work and raises defects, a reinforcing loop that shrinks feature capacity.
ideas.note: Technical debt cycle: slower and less stable.

ideas.idea: The outage is a system failure: human error is a symptom of latent organisational weaknesses, and stopping at the individual leaves them in place and breeds a false belief the problem is solved.
ideas.note: Also CAIB.

ideas.idea: Ask what in the release controls (review, testing, rollback) let one merge take the portal down for four hours; controls, not the error, set severity.
Punishing honest error drives reporting underground; a just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting culture, and blame kills learning.
ideas.note: Includes DOE blame cycle.

ideas.idea: Apply the substitution test: would comparable peers have done the same under the same conditions (here, almost certainly yes)?
Turn the review question round: how did the organisation fail the individual?
Withdraw or pause the developer's performance plan; action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate.
Rerun the postmortem as a blameless review of the system, asking what let the release through rather than who merged it.
Just culture is not blame-free: use a culpability decision tree to separate honest error from reckless or deliberate conduct, which keeps individual accountability.

Tension: sources draw the accountability line differently (NHS keeps a route to performance management, CAIB keeps personal responsibility, the Forest Service firewalls learning from discipline and redefines accountability as giving an account).
ideas.note: Claim that CAIB handled accountability 'in a separate process' was not found.

ideas.idea: Tension: traditional performance management ties rewards and sanctions to individual output, while safety science treats individual action as a product of the system.
Tension: DOE keeps root-cause analysis (aimed at prevention) while the Forest Service guide avoids causal statements in favour of networked causality.
Postmortem recommendations, once implemented, add workplace complexity and can paradoxically raise risk.
Layering new tools or structures onto an unchanged system adds complexity and new ways to fail; error risk rises at first.
Write the shared account of the outage first, then a short action list with an owner per item.
ideas.note: LFUO favours a learning product over recommendations; the owned short action list is added.

ideas.idea: The review should explain why the developer's actions made sense at the time, not what he should have done.
Buying AI tools to 'do both' is a quick fix (shifting the burden / fixes that fail) that eases symptoms and saps effort from the fundamental solution.
Writing code is not the bottleneck; improvements off the constraint are an illusion, so faster code generation into a clogged pipeline just adds WIP and review load.
ideas.note: ToC applied to the case.

ideas.idea: AI brings new human work: monitoring its output becomes an important responsibility, which overloaded squads lack time for.
If AI is bought, aim it at a specific named bottleneck (e.g. tests, review, release checks), not a generic 'adopt AI'.
Sequence AI after the flow and org-design fix, not before or instead of it.
ideas.note: Ordering follows directly from ToC plus aim-at-bottleneck premises.

ideas.idea: Tension: Org Topologies is bullish (expertise no longer scarce, 'spin up another 10,000 agents') while systems/constraint thinking warns a technical fix to a stressed system defers the real problem.
Use AI to broaden teams' skills and work mandates toward cross-functional end-to-end delivery.
'Do both' echoes NASA's 'faster, better, cheaper', which left the shuttle programme operating too close to its margins.
First change: put every developer on exactly one squad and limit work in progress.
ideas.note: Specific WIP numbers (J: 1-2 items, L: 3 epics) are not in the library.

ideas.idea: It goes first because it is the common constraint the other problems run through; other fixes inherit the overload otherwise.
ideas.note: ToC identify-the-constraint applied.

ideas.idea: It goes first because the rule is the CEO's own and org design is under leadership's control, unlike churn or the market.
It goes first because it is cheap, fast and reversible: a policy constraint that can be lifted this sprint.
ideas.note: ToC 'exploit with quick changes using existing resources'; cost and reversibility claims added.

ideas.idea: Make just culture / safety to tell the truth the first move, ahead of restructuring.
ideas.note: Prerequisite claim is in DOE; putting it ahead of the staffing change is added.

ideas.idea: Psychological safety is a prerequisite for the honest information every other change depends on.
Move the bonus suspension and postmortem reopening together with the staffing change, because one change alone will not hold.
ideas.note: Optimising one element in isolation can worsen the whole.

ideas.idea: Use the Theory of Constraints focusing cycle (identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate) to set priorities.
Keep deliberate slack: idle-looking time is what absorbs review, testing and incidents and lets work finish.
ideas.note: Library: busy people, slower work; slack as buffer and J's 15-20% figure are added.

ideas.idea: Context switching costs 20-40% of capacity; single-squad allocation recovers 20-30%.
ideas.note: No such figure in Jones or elsewhere.

ideas.idea: Reduce batch size (smaller stories, fewer in flight) so teams finish what they start faster.
Invest in automated release guardrails and quality gates (tests, review, rollback) as hard stops.
Form dedicated, stable, cross-functional squads aligned to product capabilities.
Strategy-structure mismatch: a speed ambition needs an org design for speed, not for utilisation and predictability.
Tension: Kanban says start where you are without changing roles, while Org Topologies says a team can't reach potential if surrounding structures stay unchanged.
Tension: Scrum's fixed timeboxes versus Kanban's continuous pull flow.
ideas.note: Both practices present; no source states the disagreement. I's claim that Open Kanban says sprints cause end-of-sprint rush is not in the source.

ideas.idea: Tension: classical resource-efficiency thinking (keep everyone 100% busy) versus flow thinking.
ideas.note: Attributions to OpenStax accounting/Taylorism not verified.

ideas.idea: Utilisation isn't always wrong: the Resource topology fits some purposes, just not this business.
System archetypes shouldn't be applied as labels; test the diagnosis with the squads before acting.
People must own, not rent, their change, so engineers need safety to help redesign their own work.
Top management knows about 4% of frontline problems (iceberg of ignorance), so frontline reporting matters.
Over 80% of errors behind events are latent organisational conditions, under 20% active.
ideas.note: NRC study: 81% latent, 19% active.

ideas.idea: Judge AI's net value as manual cost minus AI access, adaptation, and error detection-and-fix costs.
Offer marketing a predictable rhythm of finished features instead of a promised feature a week.
ideas.note: Follows loosely from flow and outcome-over-output sources.
